steps: Uncrate & fit the side panels

Remove the crate top, supports and plastic cover, then the lag bolts to the pallet (7/16" wrench). Hook each side panel's front tabs into the bracket slots, pull back and screw it on; use the fibre washers on enamel panels.
Connect the A/C adapter
Plug the adapter's barrel plug into the control board, then the adapter into a wall outlet. Fit the optional battery box (#11490005) per its own instructions.

If the unit is unplugged for any reason, or the power flickers and the control board freezes, unplug the adapter from the wall and wait at least 30 seconds before plugging it back in.

With the optional battery backup the appliance stays fully functional in a power failure (batteries last an estimated 5-7 days under continuous use). Without it, the stove still operates within safe and certified limits on the manual air control at the front.

When changing batteries, don't pull on the wires between the battery box and the control board.
Fit the flue thermocouple guard
Take the guard out of the flue collar, remove the cardboard holding the flue gas agitator, then refit the guard with all three ends in place.
The flue gas agitator comes pre-installed and shouldn't need handling. Do not operate the stove with the agitator removed; the replacement steps are on p. 15.
Floor protector

Continuous non-combustible ember protection: USA 16" front and 8" to the sides of the door opening; Canada 18" on the firing side and 8" on the other sides. Also under the connector, 2" beyond each side.
Chimney & connector

Listed UL-103 HT (USA) / ULC-S629 (Canada) stainless chimney or a lined masonry chimney for solid fuel, 6" flue, 15 feet minimum system height. Never share a flue; never install in a fireplace or connect to an air distribution duct.

• Chimney exit 3 feet (1 m) above the roof and two feet (0.6 m) above the highest projection within 10 feet (3 m) horizontally.
  • Single-wall connector: six inch diameter, 24 gauge black pipe, clean and in new condition, as short and straight as possible, crimped (male) ends pointing down.
  • Double-wall connector: listed (ULC S-641 in Canada, UL-103 HT in the USA); install per the chimney/connector manufacturer.
  • The connector must not pass through an attic, roof space, closet or similar concealed space, floor or ceiling. A combustible wall pass must conform to CAN/CSA-B365 or NFPA 211.
Set the stove & run the pipe
Position the floor protection and stove to the clearances, plumb-bob the ceiling and roof hole from the flue centre, check joists and rafters, then install the listed chimney and connector.

1. Position the floor protection and stove using the clearances (Figure 14, p. 19).
  2. Mark the ceiling and roof hole with a string and plumb-bob over the exact centre of the flue pipe.
  3. Check for floor joists, ceiling joists and rafters; adjust if needed and reconfirm clearances to combustibles.
  4. Install the listed chimney from the ceiling through to the rain cap per its manufacturer.
  5. Slip the crimped edge of the connector inside the stove collar and screw it through the holes provided.
  6. Add the remaining lengths up to the chimney with the manufacturer's approved adapter; a slip section makes this easier.

Venting figures: minimum 7' [2.1m] ceiling height, a minimum 12" [300mm] first section of pipe (as vertical as possible, or the unit may be harder to start), and offsets screwed with at least three sheet metal screws per joint.

Note: the manual says to secure single-wall pipe at every joint and collar with 3 sheet metal screws on p. 20, and to secure the pipe in the collar with two screws on p. 21.
Combustion air

Outside air is required for mobile homes and optional for houses (then secure the unit to the structure). Fit the 4" Intake Starter to the Ash Box Enclosure and run 4" metal flex through the floor or the wall behind.

• Through the floor: draw from a ventilated crawl space or extend with duct to the outdoors, using 4"(100mm) i.d. metal flex pipe.
  • Through the wall behind: cut the hole for a 4"(100mm) air intake and connect it to the starter with metal flex.
  • Room air: the stove draws through the opening in the Ash Box Enclosure.

Consult local code or CAN/CSA-B365 first. Anything that causes negative pressure can pull gases or fumes into the living area.
Through-wall pass (if used)
For a connector through a combustible wall, use NFPA 211-2024 System A, B, C or D, and maintain the vapor barrier wherever components penetrate to the exterior.

System A · brick and fireclay liner12 in. (305mm) to combustibles
System B · insulated factory-built chimney length9 in. (229mm)
System C · ventilated sheet steel thimble6 in. (152mm)
System D · chimney length as pass-through2 in. (51mm)

Fasteners must not penetrate the chimney flue liner. Construction details for each system are on pp. 24-25.
Mobile home specifics
Listed double-wall connector and ULC-S629 or UL-103HT chimney only, outside combustion air required, and two 1/4" x 2" or longer lag screws through the pedestal base. Not in a sleeping room.

• Use the double-wall clearances: 8" side and back wall, 5" corner (Figure 21).
  • Maintain the structural integrity of the floor, wall and ceiling/roof.
  • Remove the side panels, if installed, to fit the lag screws.
  • The rating label adds: horizontal connector not permitted in mobile homes; outside air kit required.
  • Do not connect to a chimney flue serving another appliance.
Blower kit & firebrick
Optional blower #11140001: remove the five screws on the rear heat shield cover plate, install per the kit and route the cord away from the heater. Firebrick goes in rear wall first.

The blower has a three prong power cord and can be added at any time. Don't route the cord beneath the heater.

Firebrick set #80002875

A8 7/8" x 4 3/8" x 1 1/4"
B8 7/8" x 2 1/8" x 1 1/4"
C5 3/4" x 4 3/8" x 1 1/4"
D4 7/16" x 3" x 1 1/4"
E7" x 1 3/4" x 1 1/4"

Rear wall first, then each side wall, then the floor around the ash dump (layout in Figure 22). A gap remains behind the ash dump, and one full-sized brick is left over as a spare.

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
1. Move the air control to High (all the way to the left) and open the door.
  2. Put crumpled newspaper in the centre of the stove. Crisscross several pieces of small, dry kindling over it, then add a few pieces of large kindling on top.
  3. Light the paper. Leave the door open about 1/2" to 1" until the kindling is fully in flame. Never leave the stove unattended with the door open.
  4. Once the kindling is fully engulfed, add a few small pieces of wood and close the door.
  5. When there's a good bed of coals and the wood has charred, carry on with normal burning.
Never use gasoline, kerosene, lighter fluid or any other chemical or liquid to start or freshen up a fire. Keep all such liquids well away from the stove while it is in use.

Your first few fires

The paint bakes on over the first 2-3 fires and gives off smoke and fumes. Open windows and doors so the room is well ventilated, and follow the Stove Bright (Forrest Paint) sheet that came with the stove. Smoke detectors may go off more often for a while. Don't disconnect them.

air.title: Using the air control
air.html:
The air control sits beneath the ash lip. Facing the stove, all the way left is High and to the right is Low; the middle is roughly Medium. You can set it anywhere in between for the heat you want.

  • High is for lighting and for charring fresh wood after you reload. Run it about 10 to 15 minutes, or until the wood is fully charred.
  • Low is for overnight or long burns. Char the load completely on High first, then turn the air down slowly.
Don't over-fire. Don't run on High for long stretches. A glowing red top or vent pipe means the stove is over-firing. That can permanently damage the stove and chimney and may void the warranty.

With the optional blower

When the air is on Low, set the blower to Low too, or the fire may go out. Between Low and High, any blower speed is fine. On Auto the blower starts as the stove heats up and stops after it cools; on Man it runs until you turn it off.

reload.title: Reloading and restarting
reload.html:
1. Move the air control to High and give the fire time to brighten.
  2. Open the door slowly. That keeps smoke from coming out and prevents back puffing.
  3. Load the wood parallel to the front of the stove, placed so air can flow between the pieces. Pieces can be up to 18" long.
  4. Close the door and burn on High until the new wood is charred, then set the air where you want it.

Don't load the wood so high, or in such a way, that opening the door would be hazardous. For overnight burns, unsplit logs work best.

Restarting after an overnight burn

  1. Open the door and rake the hot embers toward the front. Add a couple of dry, split logs on top and close the door.
  2. Set the air to High. The logs should start burning within a few minutes.
  3. Once the wood has charred, reset the air control.

wood.title: Choosing your wood
wood.html:
Burn natural wood only, air-dried (seasoned) for six months or more and stored under cover away from heat. Seasoned hardwood generally burns more efficiently and cleanly than softwood or freshly cut wood. Wet wood smoulders, makes heavy smoke and creosote, gives little heat and tends to go out.

Is it dry? A quick test

Put a large piece on a good bed of hot coals:

  • Dry: it's burning on more than one side within one minute.
  • Damp: it turns black and lights within three minutes.
  • Too wet: it sizzles, hisses and blackens without lighting in five minutes. Don't burn it.

A moisture meter can confirm it before you burn.

Never burn

Wet, green or unseasoned wood, treated or salt-water wood, garbage, paper products, cardboard, plywood or particleboard, coal or charcoal, anything containing plastic, rubber (tires included) or asbestos, lawn clippings or yard waste, railroad ties, manure or animal remains, construction or demolition debris, solvents, waste petroleum products, paints, paint thinners, asphalt products, and flammable fluids such as gasoline, naphtha or engine oil. Burning these materials may release toxic fumes, or make the stove ineffective and cause smoke.

Salt-water wood and garbage contain chlorides that quickly destroy metal surfaces and void the warranty. Charcoal and similar fuels can give off large amounts of carbon monoxide, a tasteless, odorless gas that can kill. Never barbecue in the stove. Fire starters made of paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

Note: The do-not-burn list (p. 6) includes wet, green and unseasoned wood, and p. 8 says to burn natural wood only, dry and well seasoned. p. 8 also says that if you feel it is necessary to burn wet or unseasoned wood, do so only with the air inlet set open enough to maintain a good strong fire and fairly high chimney temperatures, and not to attempt an overnight burn with green or wet wood. Wet wood can cause up to a 25% drop in heater output and adds significantly to creosote buildup.

ash.title: Emptying the ashes
ash.html:
Only remove ashes when the stove is cold. Once the ash is 3" to 4" deep and the fire has burned down and cooled, clear the excess, but leave about 1" on the firebox floor to help keep a hot charcoal bed.

Using the ash dump

  1. Pull the lower grill up to unlock it, then tip it toward you. The ash dump handle is behind it, under the ash lip on the left.
  2. Pull the handle out 1/2" and turn it clockwise to open the ash dump. Hold it open while you pull ashes into the opening. Leave large embers; they still hold heat.
  3. Release the handle and push it in to lock. Make sure the ash dump door is properly engaged, then fill the cavity with the remaining ash, level with the floor.
  4. Lift out the ash pan, empty it into a metal container, and seat the pan properly when you put it back.
Never burn with the ash dump open. It creates a hazardous condition.

Keep ashes in a metal container with a tight lid, on a non-combustible floor or the ground, well away from anything that burns, until the cinders are completely cool. Put no other waste in it.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
When the stove is cold, clean the glass with fireplace glass cleaner. Don't use abrasive cleaners, and never scrape it with anything that might scratch.

What the glass tells you

  • Light brown, dusty film that wipes off easily: good combustion and dry wood, so your pipes and chimney are likely fairly clean.
  • Black, greasy deposit that's hard to remove: wet or green wood and too slow a burn. The same heavy buildup is forming at least as fast in your chimney.

Still dirty with good wood? A leaking door gasket can cause it. Check the gasket and the door latch.

Protect it

Don't slam the door, and make sure no logs stick out to hit the glass. If it cracks or breaks, replace it before you use the stove again, with ceramic glass only, from your dealer.

Hot glass will cause burns. Don't touch it until it has cooled, and never let children touch it.

chimney.title: Creosote and chimney fires
chimney.html:
Slow, smoky fires leave creosote, a tar-like deposit, in the chimney. If it ignites it burns extremely hot: inside the chimney it can exceed 2000°F (1100°C).

  • Inspect the chimney connector and chimney at least once every two months in the heating season. Remove creosote once it reaches 3 mm or more.
  • Until you know your stove, check for creosote daily. Mild weather may need weekly cleaning; monthly is usually enough in the coldest months.
  • Burn dry wood with plenty of air. Don't burn wet wood (wet or green wood adds significantly to creosote), and don't turn the stove down too soon after loading.

Signs of a chimney fire

Flames and sparks shooting out of the top of the chimney, a roaring sound, or the chimney vibrating.

If it happens

  1. Get everyone ready to leave, with a plan and a meeting place outside.
  2. Close the air inlet on the stove.
  3. Call the fire department. Have a fire extinguisher handy.
  4. Before the next fire, have the chimney cleaned and checked for stress and cracks, and check combustibles around the chimney and roof.
A certified installer or chimney sweep is strongly recommended to inspect and service the chimney. Pacific Energy also strongly recommends smoke and carbon monoxide detectors in the area of the stove.

care.title: Routine checks
care.html:
Look for cracks, heavy corrosion, burned-out sections and bad warping.

WeeklyFirebrick for cracking; door gasket for sagging, placement, damage
MonthlyBrick rails and their tabs; air riser tube at the back; back of the airwash chamber; baffle locking pin
When the chimney is cleanedBaffle board and blanket; baffle and tubes; top heat shield and bolts; baffle gasket; brick rails
At least every six monthsVacuum the optional blower's grill openings

Door gasket

The door seal is a 7/8" fiberglass rope that needs only light pressure to seal, which makes it last longer. Inspect it now and then and replace it when needed; a kit is available from your dealer.

  • Some baffle warping, up to 1/4", is normal. More than that, or cracks, means it needs replacing.
  • Keep the front of the firebox, where boost air comes in, clear of built-up ash.
  • Replace broken or missing firebricks.
Call your dealer about any damage. Running the stove with broken parts can damage other parts and may void your warranty.

power.title: Power and outages
power.html:
The stove has a control board that runs on house power through a plug-in adapter.

In a power outage

  • Without the battery box: the stove still runs within safe and certified limits. Use the manual air control at the front.
  • With the optional battery box: it stays fully functional. Batteries last an estimated 5-7 days of continuous use.

If the power flickers

The control board may freeze. Unplug the adapter from the wall, wait at least 30 seconds, then plug it back in.

Changing the batteries

Gently lower the battery box so the cover faces up, release the catch and lift the cover off. Swap the batteries, refit the cover and re-engage the box. Don't pull on its wires.

Check the lights: on the control board at the back, only the blue (programmed) and green (power) lights should be on. Red means the firebox thermocouple (a heat sensor) is disconnected or not working; yellow means the same for the flue collar thermocouple. Call your dealer.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Pacific Energy's warranty covers the original registered purchaser.

Limited lifetime (10 years)Parts only: porcelain finish, glass (thermal breakage, not impact), plating, firebox, baffle
3 years comprehensiveParts and labor on any defective part for three years from the date of purchase, including blowers, speed controls and thermal switches

Not covered

  • Labor under the lifetime coverage; firebox rails and heat shields are left out of it.
  • Firebrick, gaskets and ceramic fiber blankets.
  • Misuse, abuse, improper installation, accident, lack of maintenance or modification.

Over-firing, excessive draft, heating too large an area, salt-water wood or garbage, and tampering with the air control can void it.

Register at pacificenergy.net/register with your serial number (on the certification label or the manual cover). For a claim, give your dealer proof of purchase, the purchase date, the model name and serial number.

conflicts.issue: EPA BTU output given two ways on the same page: 12,115 to 30,149 btu/hr in the Efficiency and BTU Output table, and 12,300 to 30,150 Btu/hr in the 'Under specific test conditions' statement.

Combustible alcove minimum height: rating label gives HEIGHT 6 ft / 1.83 m MIN (DEPTH 3 FT / .91 M MAX, WIDTH 41-3/4 IN / 1.06 m MIN); Figures 14 and 21 give Min. Height 7' (2.13m), Max. Depth 3' (915 mm).

Connector clearances: label D/E/F (side wall / back wall / corner to connector) = 20-1/2 / 14-3/8 / 16-7/8 in single wall and 18-1/2 / 12-3/8 / 14-7/8 in double wall. Figure 14 shows unlabelled connector figures of 20", 17 3/8", 23 1/2" (single) and 18", 15 3/8", 21 1/2" (double), about 3" larger than the label values (possibly measured to the flue centre, but the text doesn't say). Unit clearances A-C (10/10/7 and 8/8/5) agree. The label values are in the clearance table; the drawing's figures are given in the note beside them.

US floor protection at the sides: rating label lists G 16 INCHES / 405 MM (front), H 5 INCHES / 127 MM (sides), I 0 INCHES (back) for the USA; p. 18 says 16" (406 mm) to the front and 8" (203 mm) to the sides of the fuel loading door opening. May be different reference points (stove side vs door opening). Canada values agree in inches (label mm 450/200 vs p. 18 457/203).

Screws at the flue collar: p. 20 says single-wall pipe is secured at every joint and collar with 3 sheet metal screws; installation procedure step 5 on p. 21 says use the holes provided in the collar to secure the pipe with two screws.

Wet or unseasoned wood: the do-not-burn list (p. 6) names wet or green wood and unseasoned wood, and p. 8 says to burn natural wood only, dry and well seasoned; p. 8 also says "If you feel it is necessary to burn wet or unseasoned wood, do so only with the air inlet set open enough to maintain a good strong fire and fairly high chimney temperatures. Do not attempt to burn overnight using green wood or wet wood." Both shown in an amber note in the wood drawer.

catalog_mismatches.manual: 12,115 to 30,149 btu/hr (Efficiency and BTU Output table); the test statement beside it gives 12,300 to 30,150 Btu/hr

review.notes: Pages 3 (rating label / Efficiency and BTU Output table) and 18 (ember-protection figures) are scrambled in the flat text; labels and values were paired using the column positions in the manual's own layout extract (manual_pages/pages/...json): HHV tested efficiency 75%, LHV 82%, EPA BTU output 12,115 to 30,149 btu/hr, ideal/max wood length 16/18 inches; USA minimum floor protector 33" (838mm) wide x 35" (890mm) deep, Canada 43" (1.09m) x 45" (1.145m). Label floor-protection letters read as G = front, H = sides, I = back from the label drawing (BACK I / H H / FRONT G). Overall dimensions (p. 13) are an unlabeled 3-view drawing and were not transcribed; the firebrick layout (Figure 22), side-panel tabs and agitator steps rely on figures, so only the text steps are used. The manual's own cross-references are off by a page or two: the troubleshooting chart cites 'Page 8 Proper Draft' (it is on p. 9), the agitator section cites 'Baffle Removal page 10' (p. 11), the installation procedure cites the clearances diagram on 'Page 17' (p. 19), and Figure 16 cites 'Figs. 14-17' for through-wall systems (Figs. 17-20). Correct physical pages are used here. Blower amperage differs only by rounding: 115V, 60HZ, 1.0 AMP on the label (p. 3) vs 115 volts AC-1.02 amps (p. 27); both are shown, not flagged as a conflict.
